# Measurement Methodology {#sec-methods}

::: {.callout-note title="Measurement methodology · Planned"}
This chapter defines the intended measurement methodology. Implementation, clock verification, and metric validation remain pending.
:::


## Completion and clocks

CUDA work can be asynchronous with respect to the host, this means that returning from a submission call does not by itself establish completed GPU work. CUDA streams, events, and synchronization provide mechanisms for expressing and observing completion dependencies [@pytorch-cuda; @nvidia-cuda-async].

For same-host application events, we use a verified common monotonic clock domain, and keep device-event intervals separate from host timestamps.

| Symbol | Event | Required meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $c_i$ | Observation capture | Original input time and any explicit mapping into replay time |
| $r_i$ | Scheduled release | The planned arrival, preserved even if the producer fails to release the item |
| $a_i$ | Actual release | When the producer actually makes the item available |
| $g_i$ | Consumer-ready output | Host-observed readiness after required GPU work, copies, and postprocessing are complete |
| $u_i$ | Actual consumer use | Record only if observed |
| $d_i$ | Declared deadline | For a release-relative contract, $d_i=r_i+D$ |


## Preserve all offered work

We schedule workload arrivals independently of inference completion, following the distinction between open and closed workload models [@schroeder2006open].

We preserve scheduled identities and account for dropped, failed, unreleased, and unfinished work. Completed-only latency distributions are reported alongside all-outcome counts to avoid misleading performance conclusions [@tene2013latency].

Let $S$ be the set of scheduled fast items in the declared arrival cohort. The fast temporal miss fraction is:

$$
\text{Fast temporal miss fraction} =
\frac{
  \#\{i \in S : g_i \text{ is absent or } g_i > d_i\}
}{
  |S|
}
$$

Equality with the deadline counts as on time. A completed but task-incorrect output can satisfy the temporal criterion while failing the separate correctness criterion.

For this pilot, warm-up work will finish before the measurement window $[t_0,t_1)$, and its IDs will be excluded. The measured cohorts contain all frame/request IDs scheduled within that window, including items never actually released. After $t_1$, we stop offering new work but continue recording through a predeclared drain cutoff covering every cohort deadline. An unfinished item remains pending until its deadline has passed. We calculate the final miss fraction once all temporal outcomes are known; an empty cohort is reported as N/A.

## Ready latency, age, and service-valid output

**Ready latency** is $g_i-r_i$: time from scheduled release to consumer-ready output. It is analogous to response time in real-time systems, but includes producer-release lag because $r_i$ is the planned rather than the actual release [@liu2000realtime].

**Ready age** is $g_i-c_i$: the observation’s age at that boundary. This follows the timestamp-based notion of information freshness [@yates2021aoi]. 

Both quantities require comparable timestamps, with capture times mapped into the replay clock.

Motivated by SLO-aware serving metrics [@zhong2024distserve], we define a project-specific service-valid ready-output rate.

For a fixed delivery window $[t_0,t_1)$ of duration $T$ seconds, let $N_{\text{valid}}$ count unique outputs that become ready within the window and satisfy the declared correctness, deadline or expiry, and freshness requirements.

For each service separately:
$$
\text{Service-valid ready outputs per minute}
= \frac{60N_{\text{valid}}}{T}.
$$

Each original frame/request ID contributes at most once to $N_{\text{valid}}$. Outputs becoming ready during the post-window drain remain in the cohort outcome records but do not contribute to this rate. The denominator $T$ remains the measurement-window duration, excluding the drain period.

We apply the same definitions and delivery windows across applicable arms. All offered items remain in the separate outcome accounting.

Ready age is not continuous consumer Age of Information. Consumer-ready output does not imply actual consumption, and metrics at the consumer-use boundary require separately observed use events.

## Correctness, timeliness, and freshness

| Attribute | Question |
|---|---|
| Correctness | Does the output meet an independently checked task rubric? |
| Timeliness | Is the declared boundary reached by the item's deadline? |
| Freshness | Is the underlying observation recent enough at the declared boundary? |

## Slow-service outcomes

For the VLM, we account for every externally offered request, including rejected, failed, expired, and unfinished requests.

We record actual input and output work, completion outcomes, answer correctness, and freshness at the declared boundary. Service-valid output is reported separately from raw throughput.

## Fair comparisons

We use the same per-service input, arrival, and output contract across applicable arms. We preserve the same effective slow allocation in B, A-resident, and C0, with measured headroom for the fast service.

We declare warmup conditions, and use interleaved arms plus repeated-arm drift checks [@hoefler2015scientific]. Record power/thermal conditions, host load, display use, and unavailable telemetry. We compare the conditions without assuming a speciffic interference mechanism.

We measure instrumentation overhead before performance claims from the subsequent confirmatory evaluation.
